headline: Dogs can read the feelings on your face

sources.title: Brain scans show that dogs can distinguish emotions in human faces (University of Vienna)
Dogs can tell fear from sadness (ScienceDaily)
Dogs can tell when you're happy, scared or sad (The Washington Post)

chunks.text: Does your dog know when you are sad? Many [[owners]] feel that their pets can [[sense]] their [[moods]], and new [[brain scans]] point to an answer: yes, more than we thought. Scientists at the University of Vienna {{set out}} to test what really happens inside a dog's head when it looks at a human face.

verbs.correct: To begin a job with a plan
verbs.why: A young company might set out to change an entire industry, and a researcher might set out to answer one hard question. Scientists at the University of Vienna set out to test what happens inside a dog's brain when it sees a human face.

chunks.text: The team {{signed up}} 12 friendly family dogs whose owners wanted to help. Each dog {{went through}} careful [[training]] so it could [[lie still]] and [[stay awake]] inside the [[scanner]]. [[Treats]] and soft words helped the dogs {{settle down}} in the [[noisy]] machine. The researchers then {{put together}} sets of photos showing four feelings on human faces: happiness, anger, fear, and sadness.

verbs.correct: To add someone to a program
verbs.wrong: To pay someone for their work
verbs.why: A gym signs up new members every January, and a coach signs up kids for the summer soccer camp. For this study, researchers signed up 12 friendly family dogs whose owners wanted to take part.

New employees go through a week of training, and pilots go through a strict safety checklist before takeoff. Each dog in the study went through careful training so it could lie still inside the brain scanner.

verbs.wrong: To fall into a deep sleep
verbs.why: A crying baby can settle down with a soft song, and a noisy classroom can settle down once the teacher speaks. Treats and gentle words helped the dogs settle down inside the loud scanning machine.

verbs.correct: To prepare a set of things
verbs.why: A chef might put together a meal from a few simple ingredients, and a manager might put together a team for a new project. The researchers put together sets of photos showing four human feelings for the dogs to view.

chunks.text: When the dogs saw a happy face, a [[reward]] area deep in the brain {{lit up}} like a Christmas tree: the same area that becomes active for food and play. Smiles clearly matter to dogs. With help from a [[computer program]], the scans also showed that dogs could {{pick up on}} the [[difference]] between fear and sadness, two feelings that even people sometimes [[confuse]]. The brain [[pattern]] for fear {{stood out}} from the patterns for anger and sadness.

verbs.why: A child's face can light up at the sight of a birthday cake, and a dark room can light up when lightning flashes. In the scans, a reward area deep in the brain lit up whenever a dog saw a happy face.
A good friend can pick up on a small change in your mood, and a teacher can pick up on a quiet, worried student. The scans showed dogs pick up on the difference between a fearful face and a sad one.

A bright red coat stands out in a gray crowd, and one wrong answer stands out on an otherwise perfect test. In the scans, the brain pattern for fear stood out clearly from the patterns for anger and sadness.

chunks.text: The study came out this month in a science [[journal]], and it is the first clear [[evidence]] that dogs can read several human feelings in a face. Still, the scientists are careful. All the dogs were [[well-loved]] pets, and real life gives dogs much more than [[still photos]]: dogs also read [[body language]], voices, and [[smell]]. The team wants to {{follow up}} with tests closer to daily life. One thing is sure: the [[friendship]] between people and dogs {{goes back}} thousands of years, and dogs may understand us better than we knew.

verbs.why: A doctor might follow up with a phone call after surgery, and a reporter might follow up on a story with new questions. The research team wants to follow up with tests that feel closer to a dog's daily life.

verbs.correct: To have existed since a time
verbs.why: A family recipe can go back several generations, and an old friendship can go back to grade school. The bond between people and dogs goes back thousands of years, and this study shows how deep it runs.

mainIdea.s: Brain scans in Vienna show that dogs can read the feelings on human faces. A smile feels like a reward to a dog's brain, and dogs can even tell fear from sadness.
mainIdea.why: The scans showed the reward area becoming active for happy faces, with different brain patterns for fear, anger, and sadness.

mainIdea.s: Scientists in Vienna trained dogs to copy human emotions themselves. After months of practice, the dogs made happy and fearful faces of their own for the camera.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the dogs did not learn to copy feelings. The scans show their brains can tell human feelings apart.

mainIdea.s: An animal shelter in Vienna uses photos of smiling owners to help nervous dogs relax. Workers say the pictures calm the animals faster than treats or toys.
mainIdea.why: The article is about brain scans that show dogs reading faces, not about a shelter method for calming dogs.

lines.text: Science finally answered a big question: your dog really can read your face.
[[I knew it!]] My dog always knows when I'm sad.
Now there are brain scans to prove it. Researchers in Vienna {{set out}} to test what happens inside a dog's head when it looks at a human face.
How do you scan a dog's brain? They never sit still.

Training. The team {{signed up}} 12 family dogs, and each one {{went through}} careful training to lie still and stay awake in the scanner. Treats and soft words helped them {{settle down}} in the noisy machine.
[[I would watch a whole documentary about that]]. What did they show the dogs?
The researchers {{put together}} photo sets of four feelings: happiness, anger, fear, and sadness.
When a dog saw a happy face, a reward area deep in its brain {{lit up}} like a Christmas tree. The same area that reacts to food and play.

Clearly. And with a computer's help, the scans showed dogs could {{pick up on}} the difference between fear and sadness, two feelings even people confuse. The fear pattern {{stood out}} from anger and sadness.
So they know more than we thought.
The scientists stay careful. These were well-loved pets, and real life gives dogs voices, body language, and smell, not just photos. The team wants to {{follow up}} with tests closer to daily life.
Still. Thousands of years of friendship, and they've been reading us [[the whole time]].
The bond {{goes back}} that far, yes. Maybe that's why it works. [[Dogs really are something else]].
